items.text:
One idea from Rowan Cheung's newsletter, The Rundown AI, stuck with me this morning. Rowan calls it "AI intuition". Knowing when to use AI and when not to.

It immediately made me think about a pattern I've been seeing in customer conversations.

Almost every leadership team wants to talk about how AI can help them work faster, automate more, and eliminate manual work. Those are important conversations, but I'm not convinced they're the first ones we should be having.

The question I keep coming back to is where AI actually belongs.
There are parts of work that I don't think anyone will miss handing over. Summarizing meetings, chasing status updates, organizing information, finding patterns across large amounts of data, and handling repetitive coordination work are all things AI is already very good at. Every improvement there gives people more time to focus on work that actually requires them.

What I haven't seen change is the value of human judgment. Deciding where to invest, navigating disagreement between teams, building trust with customers, understanding organizational dynamics, or recognizing that a decision is technically correct but politically impossible are still deeply human skills. If anything, they become even more valuable as everything else becomes easier.

The organizations getting the most out of AI don't seem to be the ones trying to automate everything. They're the ones making thoughtful decisions about what should be automated and what shouldn't. They use AI to remove friction, not responsibility.

The models are going to keep getting better. That's a given. What I'm less certain about is whether access to better AI will be what separates organizations. I think it'll be the judgment to know where AI creates value and where people still do.

As the year wraps up I have been reflecting on just how much changed over the last twelve months both personally and professionally.

This year I became a dad to twins and everything shifted. With that came a full reset on priorities and perspective. I am genuinely grateful to ClickUp for how the company showed up during that season supporting me through paternity leave split across May and November without friction or hesitation. That level of trust and flexibility is rare and it matters.

At home none of this works without my wife. She has been the constant and the anchor carrying the weight of raising two infants with strength patience and grace. I am endlessly grateful for her.

Professionally I am proud of the team we have built and the people I get to work alongside every day. Huge thanks to leaders like Matt Bauman and Kimberly Middlemiss to partners like Sandra Palm in Solutions Engineering and Sean Hardy and Margot Moore in Professional Services. The collaboration across teams here is real and it makes the work better.

I am especially proud of our team Jake Lanier Jennifer Abramowitz Lindsay Reynolds Isabel Roche Jack Shortell and Paul Fayman. The standard they set the way they show up for customers and how they support each other is something special.

What continues to stand out to me is the culture here. From how we market and show up socially to how rapidly we innovate internally we are not afraid to try things. We move fast we learn quickly and we iterate without ego. That mindset is refreshing and it shows up everywhere.

And then there is the timing of all this. Watching ClickUp launch Super Agents last week and hearing our leaders talk about what it really means to adapt AI to how humans work was a reminder of how unique it is to be building at the cutting edge of this space. It is rare to work somewhere where the ambition is this high and the execution backs it up.

Looking ahead to next year I am genuinely excited. About the team. About where ClickUp is headed. About continuing to build meaningful things with people who care about getting it right.

Grateful for this year. Ready for the next one.

ClickUp blew past the $300mn ARR milestone. This, while staying super efficient 💥 
 
When I joined ClickUp, I knew we had the potential to do something extraordinary. Today we announce that ClickUp has reached $300 million in ARR. This is a moment to celebrate, but it’s also a moment to reflect on how we got here.
 
For me, it’s always been about building for the long game. Scaling isn’t just about growth—it’s about creating systems that last, fostering a culture of accountability, and staying true to our mission of making work more productive. 

That’s why we’ve invested in a Converged AI Workspace —ensuring our teams have a unified, intelligent platform to support sustainable success.
 
This milestone is a credit to the incredible team at ClickUp. From the early days of scrappy problem-solving to today’s AI-powered operations, we’ve never stopped pushing ourselves to be better.
 
The journey is far from over. With the foundation we’ve built, I’m more excited than ever about what’s ahead. Here’s to the next chapter and to everyone who’s been part of this ride.
